title: Baker County, North Powder fifth graders learn about food systems at Field to Fork - NewsBreak
text:
By Lisa Britton ,
23 hours ago 1/2 Bryanna Carney, 4-H program coordinator for Baker County, watches as South Baker fifth graders Aubrey Fields, left, and Hadley Jacobs plant a garden in a glove during Field to Fork on May 6, 2026. Chelsie Thompson, back, was one of the high school volunteers. (Lisa Britton/Baker City Herald) BAKER CITY — Bryanna Carney grinned as she watched kids build soil layers with pudding, and plant seeds in a plastic glove, and learn about the water cycle.
“I would have loved a field trip like this when I was in elementary school,” she said of the 2026 Field to Fork program at the Baker County Fairgrounds.
Carney started her job as the Baker County 4-H coordinator in September 2025. Part of her position is to oversee Field to Fork on May 6-7, which welcomed 170 fifth graders from Baker City, North Powder, Haines, Keating, Halfway, Unity and Huntington.
The object is to help kids understand the food cycle, and how their bread or burger gets from the field to their fork.
The program started nearly 20 years ago, and is organized by the Baker County Farm Bureau and OSU Extension Service in Baker County. Volunteers spent each day teaching stations on commodities, water, soil, harvest and growing a garden in a glove.
“This is such an awesome opportunity for the kids,” Carney said. “The volunteers who help make it happen are amazing — we couldn’t do it without them.”
Volunteers come from across the community, as well as high school leadership classes, FFA programs in Baker and North Powder, and 4-H Ambassadors. Every year, the Baker County Cattlewomen serve a lunch of beef sandwiches, carrots, apples, baked potatoes and ice cream.
Additional help this year came from AgWest Farm Credit, which supported Field to Fork through its Team Giving program. Mark Coomer, branch manager in Baker City, said AgWest donated $2,000 to the program — $400 per each of the five staff members who volunteered their time.
New 4-H coordinator Carney grew up in Washington’s Puget Sound area, where she worked with horses. However, her grandparents owned a cattle ranch in Western Oregon.
“I spent a lot of time there,” she said.
She joined FFA in high school, and attended Fresno State University for ag education, with an animal science emphasis. She also competed on the equestrian team.
She was surrounded by agriculture while at college in California’s Central Valley.
“All the fruit and produce you’ll ever want,” she said.
She graduated in 2024, and worked as a supervisor at Foster Farms, then later at a feedlot in Madras. Then she applied for the 4-H job in Baker City.
“I like the focus of agriculture,” she said.
Plus, it’s a challenge.
“It’s something completely different for me,” she said.
In her role, Carney manages 4-H clubs and volunteers, as well as Field to Fork and the annual Christmas bazaar in December. She’s hoping to add more school programs in the future.
For information about 4-H in Baker County, contact Carney at 541-523-6418 or email bryanna.carney@oregonstate.edu.
